proofs.proof_tex:
Write
\[
 \kappa_X^2=\sup_x k(x,x)<\infty,
 \qquad
 \kappa_Y^2=\sup_y\ell(y,y)<\infty.
 \tag{1}
\]
The two finiteness statements in (1) are respectively the bounded-covariate-kernel and bounded-outcome-kernel assumptions.  By the reproducing property, \(\|K_x\|_{\mathcal H_X}\leq\kappa_X\) and \(\|L_y\|_{\mathcal H_Y}\leq\kappa_Y\).  In particular, every Hilbert-valued score in the corrected construction has a finite second moment.

We first prove the upper bound.  For \(a\in\{0,1\}\), define
\[
 D_a=\mathbf 1\{A=a\},
 \qquad
 \pi_a(x)=P(D_a=1\mid X=x),
 \qquad
 p_a(x)=\pi_a(x)^{-1},
 \qquad
 \mu_a(dx)=\pi_a(x)P_X(dx).
 \tag{2}
\]
The overlap assumption gives \(\eta\leq\pi_a\leq1-\eta\).  The density-band assumption therefore gives
\[
 \eta c_X\leq\frac{d\mu_a}{dx}\leq(1-\eta)C_X.
 \tag{3}
\]
The propensity Hölder assumption and the fact that inversion is smooth on \([\eta,1-\eta]\) imply
\[
 p_a\in\mathcal H^{\beta_e}(C_p)
 \tag{4}
\]
for a finite constant \(C_p\) depending only on \(\eta,\beta_e,L_e\).  This follows directly by repeatedly applying the product rule to \(\pi_a p_a=1\) through order \(\lfloor\beta_e\rfloor\), and then applying the Hölder difference inequality to the highest derivative.  Thus (4) uses no smoothness of \(f_X\).

Let \(\mathcal S_M\) and \(z_M\) be as in the corrected construction.  On each dyadic cell, Taylor's formula with Hölder remainder gives a polynomial \(s_f\in\mathcal S_M\) satisfying
\[
 \sup_x|p_a(x)-s_{p,a}(x)|\leq C M^{-\beta_e/d},
 \qquad
 \sup_x\|\nu_a(x)-s_{\nu,a}(x)\|_{\mathcal H_Y}
 \leq C M^{-\beta_m/d}.
 \tag{5}
\]
The second inequality is the same Taylor identity with Hilbert-valued derivatives; the triangle inequality in \(\mathcal H_Y\) bounds its integral remainder.  Hence it follows from (3), (4), and the outcome Hölder assumption.  Let \(\Pi_{a,M}\) be orthogonal projection in \(L^2(\mu_a)\), acting componentwise on Hilbert-valued functions.  Its best-approximation property and (5) yield
\[
 \|(I-\Pi_{a,M})(1-p_a)\|_{L^2(\mu_a)}\leq C M^{-\beta_e/d},
 \qquad
 \|(I-\Pi_{a,M})\nu_a\|_{L^2(\mu_a;\mathcal H_Y)}
 \leq C M^{-\beta_m/d}.
 \tag{6}
\]

Put
\[
 \Omega_a=\int z_M(x)z_M(x)^\top\,d\mu_a(x).
 \tag{7}
\]
Because the coordinates of \(z_M\) are orthonormal in \(L^2(dx)\), (3) implies the operator inequalities
\[
 \eta c_X I_M\preceq\Omega_a\preceq(1-\eta)C_X I_M.
 \tag{8}
\]
The local polynomial basis has a fixed number of nonzero coordinates at each \(x\), and rescaling a fixed reference-cell basis gives
\[
 \sup_x\|z_M(x)\|_2^2\leq C_BM.
 \tag{9}
\]
Here \(C_B\) depends only on \(d\) and the fixed polynomial degree.

We record the empirical-Gram bounds needed below and derive them from (8)--(9).  For a Gram half of size \(N\asymp n\), put \(\Delta_a=\Omega_a-\widehat\Omega_{a,G}\).  Both matrices are block diagonal with blocks of a fixed size, one block for each dyadic cell.  For a fixed entry of a block, the centered summand is bounded by \(CM\), has variance at most \(CM\), and is nonzero off its mean only when the covariate falls in that cell.  For \(|\lambda|<3/(CM)\), the elementary inequality
\[
 e^u\leq1+u+\frac{u^2}{2(1-|u|/3)}
 \tag{10}
\]
and independence imply the scalar Bernstein bound
\[
 P\{|\widehat\Omega_{a,G}^{uv}-\Omega_a^{uv}|>x\}
 \leq2\exp\left\{-\frac{cNx^2}{M+Mx}\right\}.
 \tag{11}
\]
There are at most \(C M\) nonzero within-block entries.  A union bound, equivalence of entrywise and operator norms on each fixed-size block, and integration of (11) give, for every fixed integer \(j\geq1\),
\[
 P(\mathcal E_{a,G}^c)\leq CM\exp(-cN/M),
 \qquad
 E\big[\mathbf1_{\mathcal E_{a,G}}\|\Delta_a\|_{\mathrm{op}}^{2j}\big]
 \leq C_j\left(\frac{M\log n}{N}\right)^j.
 \tag{12}
\]
All constants in (12) are uniform over the density band; no derivative of \(f_X\) was used.

We next compute the conditional bias exactly.  Conditional on the Gram half, define
\[
 \mathcal A_{a,q}
 =\sum_{\ell=0}^{q-1}(-1)^\ell
 \widehat\Omega_{a,G}^{-1}
 (\Delta_a\widehat\Omega_{a,G}^{-1})^\ell,
 \qquad
 Q_{a,q}f=z_M^\top\mathcal A_{a,q}\int z_M f\,d\mu_a.
 \tag{13}
\]
The estimation half is independent of the Gram half by the independent-sampling assumption.  Moreover, for \(R_a^p=D_a-1\) and \(R_a^\nu=D_aL_Y\), definitions (2) give
\[
 E[z_MR_a^p]=\int z_M(1-p_a)\,d\mu_a,
 \qquad
 E[z_M\otimes R_a^\nu]=\int z_M\otimes\nu_a\,d\mu_a,
 \qquad
 E[D_ah(X)]=\int h\,d\mu_a.
 \tag{14}
\]
Also \(E[G_{a,i}\mid G]=\Delta_a\).  Since every \(U\)-statistic in the construction uses distinct estimation-half indices, repeated use of independence and (14) shows
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 E[C^{(1)}_{a,\ell}\mid G]
 &=\int K_x\otimes\nu_a(x)\,
 z_M(x)^\top\widehat\Omega_{a,G}^{-1}
 (\Delta_a\widehat\Omega_{a,G}^{-1})^\ell
 \left\{\int z_M(1-p_a)\,d\mu_a\right\},d\mu_a(x),\\
 E[C^{(2)}_{a,\ell}\mid G]
 &=\int K_x\otimes
 \left[z_M(x)^\top\widehat\Omega_{a,G}^{-1}
 (\Delta_a\widehat\Omega_{a,G}^{-1})^\ell
 \left\{\int z_M\otimes\nu_a\,d\mu_a\right\}\right]
 (1-p_a(x))\,d\mu_a(x).
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{15}
\]
The two branches in \(C^{(3)}_{a,\ell,r}\) similarly give the product of the two bracketed projected functions at their common anchor.  Summing the signs in the definition of \(\mathcal C_{a,q}^{I\mid G}\), and observing that
\[
 E[D_aK_X\otimes L_Y]-E[K_X\otimes\nu_a(X)]
 =\int K_x\otimes(1-p_a(x))\nu_a(x)\,d\mu_a(x),
 \tag{16}
\]
therefore gives the exact inclusion--exclusion identity
\[
 E[\widehat\theta_a^{I\mid G}\mid G]-E[K_X\otimes\nu_a(X)]
 =\int K_x\otimes
 \{(I-Q_{a,q})(1-p_a)\}(x)
 \{(I-Q_{a,q})\nu_a\}(x)\,d\mu_a(x).
 \tag{17}
\]
This is the step that is absent from the scalar unweighted projection argument: the two one-sided terms and the common-anchor term make (17) valid without any smoothness of \(x\mapsto K_x\).

On \(\mathcal E_{a,G}\), (8) and the finite Neumann identity imply
\[
 \|\mathcal A_{a,q}-\Omega_a^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \leq C_q\|\Delta_a\|_{\mathrm{op}}^q.
 \tag{18}
\]
For scalar or Hilbert-valued \(f\), (7)--(8), Cauchy--Schwarz, and (18) imply
\[
 \|(Q_{a,q}-\Pi_{a,M})f\|_{L^2(\mu_a)}
 \leq C_q\|\Delta_a\|_{\mathrm{op}}^q\|f\|_{L^2(\mu_a)}.
 \tag{19}
\]
Apply (19) to \(1-p_a\) and \(\nu_a\), whose norms are uniformly bounded by overlap and (1), and combine it with (6).  The norm of the right side of (17) is at most
\[
 C\big\{M^{-\beta_e/d}+\|\Delta_a\|_{\mathrm{op}}^q\big\}
   \big\{M^{-\beta_m/d}+\|\Delta_a\|_{\mathrm{op}}^q\big\},
 \tag{20}
\]
because \(\|K_x\|\leq\kappa_X\) and Cauchy--Schwarz applies in \(L^2(\mu_a)\).

For completeness, we also give the second-moment calculation for the Hilbert-valued \(U\)-statistics.  If an order-\(j\) kernel is averaged over distinct indices, two summands with disjoint index sets are independent; if exactly \(c\) indices overlap, their number divided by \((N)_j^2\) is at most \(C_jN^{-c}\).  Repeatedly integrating a nonshared endpoint uses (7), while a shared endpoint uses
\[
 \iint |z_M(x)^\top Bz_M(x')|^2\,d\mu_a(x)d\mu_a(x')
 =\operatorname{tr}(B\Omega_aB^\top\Omega_a)
 \leq C M\|B\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2.
 \tag{21}
\]
Boundedness in (1), \(|R_a^p|\leq1\), (8), and the inverse bound on \(\mathcal E_{a,G}\) show inductively that a covariance with \(c\) shared indices is at most \(C_qM^{c-1}\).  Every kernel in the construction has order at most \(2q+3\); hence the overlap enumeration and (21) give
\[
 E\left[\left\|\widehat\theta_a^{I\mid G}
 -E(\widehat\theta_a^{I\mid G}\mid G)\right\|_{\mathcal H}^2
 \mathbf1_{\mathcal E_{0,G}\cap\mathcal E_{1,G}}\right]
 \leq\frac{C_q}{N}\sum_{c=1}^{2q+3}\left(\frac{M}{N}\right)^{c-1}
 \leq\frac{2C_q}{N}
 \tag{22}
\]
for all large \(n\).  Identity (21) is unchanged for Hilbert-valued endpoints: after expanding a squared norm, scalar products replace scalar products of outcomes, and their absolute values are bounded by (1).  Thus (22) is a Hilbert-norm bound, not a coordinatewise assertion.

Choose \(M\asymp n^\gamma\).  The two choices imposed in the construction give
\[
 M^{-2t/d}=o(n^{-1}),
 \qquad
 \left(\frac{M\log n}{n}\right)^q=o(n^{-1}),
 \qquad
 M/n=o(1).
 \tag{23}
\]
Squaring (20), applying (12) with \(j=q\) and \(j=2q\), and using (23) proves that the squared conditional bias is \(o(n^{-1})\), uniformly in \(P\in\mathcal M\).  On the complement of the stable-Gram event the directed estimator is zero, while
\[
 \|\Psi(P)\|_{\mathcal H}
 \leq E\|K_X\|\,\|\nu_1(X)-\nu_0(X)\|
 \leq2\kappa_X\kappa_Y.
 \tag{24}
\]
The first bound in (12), (23), and (24) show that this exceptional event contributes \(o(n^{-1})\) to squared risk.  Jensen's inequality for the average of the two directions, (20)--(24), and the two arms now yield
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal M}E_P
 \|\widehat\Psi_n^{\mathrm{ho}}-\Psi(P)\|_{\mathcal H}^2
 \leq \frac{C}{n}
 \tag{25}
\]
for all sufficiently large \(n\).  Each of the finitely many remaining sample sizes has finite risk because the stabilized inverse is uniformly bounded and every displayed \(U\)-statistic has finite order.  Consequently the explicit constant \(V_\star\) in the corrected construction is finite.

Under \(P\in\mathcal M_0\), \(\Psi(P)=0\) by the definition of the null class.  Markov's inequality and the definition of \(V_\star\) give
\[
 E_P\varphi_n^{\mathrm{ho}}
 \leq \frac{nE_P\|\widehat\Psi_n^{\mathrm{ho}}-\Psi(P)\|^2}{V_\star/\alpha}
 <\alpha.
 \tag{26}
\]
If
\[
 \|\Psi(P)\|_{\mathcal H}\geq
 C_{\alpha,\beta}n^{-1/2},
 \qquad
 C_{\alpha,\beta}=\sqrt{V_\star}\left(\alpha^{-1/2}+\beta^{-1/2}\right),
 \tag{27}
\]
then failure to reject and the reverse triangle inequality imply
\[
 \|\widehat\Psi_n^{\mathrm{ho}}-\Psi(P)\|_{\mathcal H}
 \geq\sqrt{V_\star/(\beta n)}.
\]
Another application of Markov's inequality yields
\[
 E_P(1-\varphi_n^{\mathrm{ho}})<\beta.
 \tag{28}
\]
Equations (26)--(28) are stronger than the asserted \(\alpha+o(1)\) and \(\beta+o(1)\) bounds.  They hold uniformly over the source-constrained alternatives because the proof used only membership in \(\mathcal M\).  The definition of \(\delta_n^\star\) therefore gives
\[
 \delta_n^\star\leq C_{\alpha,\beta}n^{-1/2}.
 \tag{29}
\]

We finally prove the conditional reverse inequality.  Assume the class-richness premise in the theorem.  Since \(P_X\) is fixed along the path and \(U_{P_\theta}(x)=\theta b_Y\), the definition of \(\Psi\) gives, equation by equation,
\[
 \Psi(P_\theta)
 =E_{P_\theta}[K_X\otimes U_{P_\theta}(X)]
 =\theta E_{P_0}[K_X]\otimes b_Y
 =\theta w_0.
 \tag{30}
\]
Let
\[
 B_s=\sup_{|\theta|\leq\varepsilon_0}
 \sum_{j\geq1}\mu_j(P_\theta)^{-2s}
 |\langle w_0,v_j(P_\theta)\rangle_{\mathcal H}|^2<\infty.
 \tag{31}
\]
For \(\theta_n=c_0n^{-1/2}\), (30)--(31) imply
\[
 \sum_{j\geq1}\mu_j(P_{\theta_n})^{-2s}
 |\langle\Psi(P_{\theta_n}),v_j(P_{\theta_n})\rangle|^2
 \leq c_0^2B_s/n\leq R^2
 \tag{32}
\]
for all sufficiently large \(n\).  Because the path is contained in \(\mathcal M\), (30), (32), and \(w_0\neq0\) show
\[
 P_{\theta_n}\in\mathcal M_1(\delta_n;s,R),
 \qquad
 \delta_n=c_0\|w_0\|_{\mathcal H}n^{-1/2}.
 \tag{33}
\]

Quadratic-mean differentiability supplies a score \(\dot\ell\in L^2_0(P_0)\) with Fisher information \(I=E_{P_0}\dot\ell^2\in(0,\infty)\) and
\[
 \int\left(
 \sqrt{dP_\theta}-\sqrt{dP_0}
 -\frac{\theta}{2}\dot\ell\sqrt{dP_0}
 \right)^2=o(\theta^2).
 \tag{34}
\]
Consequently, for the squared Hellinger distance \(H^2(P,Q)=\int(\sqrt{dP}-\sqrt{dQ})^2\),
\[
 H^2(P_\theta,P_0)=\frac{I\theta^2}{4}+o(\theta^2).
 \tag{35}
\]
The product-affinity identity gives
\[
 H^2(P_{\theta_n}^{\otimes n},P_0^{\otimes n})
 =2\left[1-\left\{1-\frac12H^2(P_{\theta_n},P_0)\right\}^{n}\right]
 \leq nH^2(P_{\theta_n},P_0).
 \tag{36}
\]
By Cauchy--Schwarz applied to \(|p-q|=|\sqrt p-\sqrt q|(\sqrt p+\sqrt q)\),
\[
 \operatorname{TV}(P,Q)=\frac12\int|p-q|
 \leq H(P,Q).
 \tag{37}
\]
Equations (35)--(37) show that the total variation distance between the two product laws is at most \(C_Ic_0+o(1)\).  Since \(\beta<1-\alpha\), choose \(c_0>0\) so small that this bound is strictly below \(1-\alpha-\beta\) for all large \(n\).  For any randomized test \(\varphi_n\) with \(E_{P_0}\varphi_n\leq\alpha\), the defining variational inequality for total variation gives
\[
 E_{P_{\theta_n}}(1-\varphi_n)
 \geq1-E_{P_0}\varphi_n
 -\operatorname{TV}(P_{\theta_n}^{\otimes n},P_0^{\otimes n})
 >\beta.
 \tag{38}
\]
Thus no level-\(\alpha\) test has type-II error at most \(\beta\) on \(\mathcal M_1(\delta_n;s,R)\).  Monotonicity of the alternative classes in \(\delta\), the definition of \(\delta_n^\star\), and (33) imply
\[
 \delta_n^\star\geq c_0\|w_0\|_{\mathcal H}n^{-1/2}.
 \tag{39}
\]
Combining (29) and (39) proves \(\delta_n^\star\asymp n^{-1/2}\) under the stated class-richness premise.

proposed_definition_changes.proposed:
Fix a number \(\gamma\) with \(d/(2t)<\gamma<1\), and fix an integer \(q\geq1\) such that \(q(1-\gamma)>1\).  Let \(\mathcal S_M\) be the space of periodic, cellwise tensor polynomials of coordinate degree at most \(p>\max\{\beta_e,\beta_m\}\) on a regular dyadic partition, and let \(z_M(x)\in\mathbb R^M\) be an \(L^2(dx)\)-orthonormal local basis of \(\mathcal S_M\), including the constant function.  Take the closest admissible dimension \(M=M_n\asymp n^\gamma\), and set the declared approximation rank to \(M_{\mathrm{proj}}=M\), so \(M_{\mathrm{proj}}=o(n)\).  Split the sample into two sets \(I,G\) of comparable sizes.  The following defines the directed estimator based on estimation set \(I\) and Gram set \(G\); the final estimator averages this construction with the roles of \(I,G\) reversed.

For \(a\in\{0,1\}\), put \(D_{a,i}=\mathbf 1\{A_i=a\}\), \(z_i=z_M(X_i)\),
\[
 \widehat\Omega_{a,G}=|G|^{-1}\sum_{i\in G}D_{a,i}z_i z_i^\top,
 \qquad
 \mathcal E_{a,G}=\left\{\lambda_{\min}(\widehat\Omega_{a,G})\geq\frac{\eta c_X}{2},\ 
 \lambda_{\max}(\widehat\Omega_{a,G})\leq2C_X\right\}.
\]
On \(\mathcal E_{a,G}\), set \(B_{a,G}=\widehat\Omega_{a,G}^{-1}\) and
\[
 G_{a,i}=D_{a,i}z_i z_i^\top-\widehat\Omega_{a,G},
 \qquad R^p_{a,i}=D_{a,i}-1,
 \qquad R^\nu_{a,i}=D_{a,i}L_{Y_i}.
\]
For \(\ell\geq0\), define
\[
 A_{a,\ell}(i_1,\ldots,i_\ell)
 =B_{a,G}\prod_{u=1}^{\ell}(G_{a,i_u}B_{a,G}),
 \qquad A_{a,0}=B_{a,G}.
\]
For a displayed kernel whose indices are all distinct, let \(\mathbb{U}_I\) denote its ordered, without-replacement average over \(I\).  Define
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 C^{(1)}_{a,\ell}
 &=\mathbb{U}_I\!\left[
  (K_{X_{i_0}}\otimes R^\nu_{a,i_0})
  \{z_{i_0}^\top A_{a,\ell}(i_1,\ldots,i_\ell)z_{i_{\ell+1}}\}
  R^p_{a,i_{\ell+1}}
 \right],\\
 C^{(2)}_{a,\ell}
 &=\mathbb{U}_I\!\left[
  (K_{X_{i_0}}\otimes R^\nu_{a,i_{\ell+1}})
  R^p_{a,i_0}
  \{z_{i_0}^\top A_{a,\ell}(i_1,\ldots,i_\ell)z_{i_{\ell+1}}\}
 \right].
 \end{aligned}
\]
For \(0\leq\ell,r<q\), put \(j=\ell+r+2\) and define the two-branch term
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 C^{(3)}_{a,\ell,r}=\mathbb{U}_I\!\Big[&
 D_{a,i_0}(K_{X_{i_0}}\otimes R^\nu_{a,i_j})
 \{z_{i_0}^\top A_{a,\ell}(i_1,\ldots,i_\ell)z_{i_{\ell+1}}\}
 R^p_{a,i_{\ell+1}}\\
 &\times
 \{z_{i_0}^\top A_{a,r}(i_{\ell+2},\ldots,i_{\ell+r+1})z_{i_j}\}
 \Big].
 \end{aligned}
\]
The arm correction and directed arm estimator are
\[
 \mathcal C_{a,q}^{I\mid G}
 =\sum_{\ell=0}^{q-1}(-1)^\ell\{C^{(1)}_{a,\ell}+C^{(2)}_{a,\ell}\}
 -\sum_{\ell,r=0}^{q-1}(-1)^{\ell+r}C^{(3)}_{a,\ell,r},
 \qquad
 \widehat\theta_a^{I\mid G}
 =|I|^{-1}\sum_{i\in I}D_{a,i}K_{X_i}\otimes L_{Y_i}-\mathcal C_{a,q}^{I\mid G}.
\]
If either \(\mathcal E_{0,G}\) or \(\mathcal E_{1,G}\) fails, set the corresponding directed contrast to zero.  Otherwise set
\[
 \widehat\Psi^{I\mid G}=\widehat\theta_1^{I\mid G}-\widehat\theta_0^{I\mid G},
 \qquad
 \widehat\Psi_n^{\mathrm{ho}}=\frac12\left(\widehat\Psi^{I\mid G}+\widehat\Psi^{G\mid I}\right).
\]
For the finitely many \(n\) smaller than the largest displayed \(U\)-statistic order, take every unavailable correction to be zero.  Finally define the deterministic class constant
\[
 V_\star=1+\sup_{m\geq1}\sup_{P\in\mathcal M}
 mE_P\|\widehat\Psi_m^{\mathrm{ho}}-\Psi(P)\|_{\mathcal H}^2.
\]
The proof of the high-smoothness theorem shows \(V_\star<\infty\).  The associated test is the explicit sample map
\[
 \varphi_n^{\mathrm{ho}}
 =\mathbf 1\left\{\|\widehat\Psi_n^{\mathrm{ho}}\|_{\mathcal H}>sqrt{\frac{V_\star}{\alpha n}}\right\}.
\]
proposed_definition_changes.reason: The frozen handle was not a sample map and omitted the weighted projection terms needed for an RKHS-valued target. The corrected construction gives the split, local basis, stabilized empirical arm Gram matrices, all ordered U-statistic kernels, the finite Neumann order, the cross-fit average, and the critical value. Its two one-sided terms and common-anchor term leave an exact product of projection residuals without requiring smoothness of the kernel feature map or the design density.
